Get your Mac's memory back.** **English** · [Español](README.es.md) [![Version](https://img.shields.io/badge/version-1.2.1-047857?style=flat-square)](https://github.com/eriktaveras/modelnap/releases/latest) ![macOS](https://img.shields.io/badge/macOS-14%2B-111?style=flat-square&logo=apple&logoColor=white) ![Architecture](https://img.shields.io/badge/Apple%20Silicon%20%7C%20Intel-universal-111?style=flat-square) ![Swift](https://img.shields.io/badge/Swift-AppKit%20%2B%20SwiftUI-F05138?style=flat-square&logo=swift&logoColor=white) ![Notarized](https://img.shields.io/badge/Apple-signed%20%26%20notarized-34D399?style=flat-square&logo=apple&logoColor=white) ![Languages](https://img.shields.io/badge/languages-EN%20%7C%20ES-5C6B64?style=flat-square) [![MIT License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-047857?style=flat-square)](LICENSE) [![Build](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/eriktaveras/modelnap/build.yml?branch=main&style=flat-square&label=build)](https://github.com/eriktaveras/modelnap/actions/workflows/build.yml) [Website](https://modelnap.com) · [Download](https://github.com/eriktaveras/modelnap/releases/latest) · [Features](#-features) · [Install](#-install) · [How it works](#%EF%B8%8F-how-it-works) · [Development](#%EF%B8%8F-development) · [Contributing](#-contributing) ## Why? A 20–30 GB local model stays in RAM even when you're not using it. Turning Ollama off isn't obvious either: it depends on how it was installed, and if you do it the wrong way, macOS starts it again on its own. **ModelNap** lets the model sleep when you don't need it and gives you one-click control over Ollama, no Terminal required. ## ✨ Features | | Feature | Details | |:-:|---|---| | ⏻ | **Turn on and off** | A button in the panel, or **⌥⌘O** from any app. | | 🔍 | **Detects your install** | Ollama.app, `brew services`, your own LaunchAgent or a manual `ollama serve`. It stops Ollama the same way it starts. | | 🧹 | **Frees idle memory** | After 5, 15, 30 or 60 minutes without generating, it unloads the model. Ollama stays on and reloads it with the next message. | | 📊 | **Mac memory** | RAM in use (same calculation as Activity Monitor), how much of it is the model, and the system's memory pressure. | | 🗂️ | **Installed models** | Size, quantization and *vision* / *tools* tags. Load or free any of them in one click. | | 🟢 | **Status at a glance** | The logo in the menu bar, with a green, amber or no dot. | | 🌍 | **English and Spanish** | Follows the system language, or pick one in Settings. | | 🌗 | **Light and dark** | Matches your macOS appearance. | | 🔒 | **Private** | Only talks to Ollama on your Mac. No accounts, no telemetry, no analytics. | | 🧾 | **Open source** | MIT licensed: you can check exactly what it does. | ## 📥 Install 1. Download **`ModelNap-1.2.1.dmg`** from [Releases](https://github.com/eriktaveras/modelnap/releases/latest). 2. Open it and drag the app to **Applications**. 3. Launch it: it shows up in the **menu bar, top right**. > [!NOTE] > The app and the installer are **signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple**, so they open without Gatekeeper warnings. > To verify the download: `shasum -a 256 -c ModelNap-1.2.1.dmg.sha256` **Requirements:** macOS 14 Sonoma or later · Apple Silicon or Intel · [Ollama](https://ollama.com/download) installed. ## 🧭 Usage ### In the menu bar | Action | Result | |---|---| | **Click** the icon | Opens the panel | | **Right-click** | Turn on/off, view the Ollama log, open at login, *About*, quit | | **⌥⌘O** | Turns Ollama on or off from any app | ### Settings From the gear in the panel: - **Free memory when idle** — never, 5, 15, 30 or 60 min. - **Keyboard shortcut** — turn ⌥⌘O on or off. - **Open at login** — the app asks the first time and never adds itself. - **Language** — automatic, English or Spanish. ## ⚙️ How it works ### Stopping Ollama the right way Killing the process doesn't always work: a LaunchAgent with `KeepAlive` brings it right back. ModelNap detects the mechanism and uses its own. | If Ollama comes from… | Stop | Start | Verified | |---|---|---|:-:| | **Ollama.app** (ollama.com) | Quits the app | Opens the app | ⏳ pending | | **`brew services`** or your own LaunchAgent | `launchctl bootout` | `launchctl bootstrap` | ✅ | | **Manual `ollama serve`** | `SIGTERM` to the server | Launches `ollama serve` | ✅ | | **Not installed** | — | Opens ollama.com/download | ✅ | Detection order: running Ollama.app → loaded LaunchAgent → standalone `ollama serve` → whatever is installed. While Ollama is off, it remembers the last mechanism it was running with. ### Detecting an idle model Ollama doesn't expose when the last request happened. Each loaded model runs in an `ollama runner` process that only uses CPU while it's working: | Measurement (gemma4 26B, Apple M5 Pro) | Runner CPU time | |---|---:| | 30 s idle | +0.06 s | | Generating 104 tokens | +0.99 s | Every 2.5 s the app adds up the runners' CPU time (`

items.title: carldaws/hunch
items.raw: # Hunch Probabilistic control flow for Ruby. Hunch lets you ask questions about text or application data and use the answers in your Ruby code. ```ruby if Hunch.almost_certainly?("this order is fraudulent", given: order.attributes) order.hold! end ``` You can get a probability, choose between options, or rate something on a scale. Questions are written in plain English; answers come back as Ruby values. Hunch uses [TypeSafe's Jev](https://typesafe.ai). You can call it directly or through OpenRouter. ## Installation ```ruby gem "hunch" ``` ```ruby Hunch.configure do |config| config.api_key = ENV["TYPESAFE_API_KEY"] end ``` ## Usage **`chance`** returns a probability between 0 and 1: ```ruby Hunch.chance("written by a real human, not spam", given: bio) # => 0.87 ``` Use a named threshold when you want a boolean: ```ruby Hunch.possibly?("fraudulent", given: order) # chance >= 0.25 Hunch.likely?("fraudulent", given: order) # chance >= 0.5 Hunch.probably?("fraudulent", given: order) # chance >= 0.75 Hunch.almost_certainly?("fraudulent", given: order) # chance >= 0.93 Hunch.configure { |c| c.levels[:definitely] = 0.99 } Hunch.definitely?("fraudulent", given: order) # chance >= 0.99 ``` Configure built-in thresholds with the matching level names, for example `Hunch.configure { |c| c.levels[:probably] = 0.8 }`. **`pick`** chooses one of the options you provide: ```ruby Hunch.pick(:ham, :spam, given: email) # => :spam Hunch.pick(urgent: "needs a reply today", routine: "can wait", given: ticket) # => :routine ``` **`rate`** returns a rating with a position on an ordered scale: ```ruby mood = Hunch.rate(:calm, :frustrated, :livid, given: email) mood.level # => :frustrated mood.position # => 1.4 mood >= :livid # => false ``` Use `pick` for categories such as billing, support, and sales. Use `rate` for ordered levels such as low, medium, and high. Both accept symbols or `symbol: "description"` pairs, or a mix of the two. Add `question:` if the options need more context. `given:` supplies the data to evaluate. These two keywords are reserved and can't be used as option names. ## Batching Use `Hunch.decide` to ask several questions about the same data in one API call: ```ruby result = Hunch.decide(given: mail.raw_source) do |q| q.probably? :urgent, "does this convey urgency?" q.pick :team, billing: "payments", technical: "bugs", sales: "pricing" q.rate :mood, :calm, :frustrated, :livid end result.urgent # => 0.92 result.urgent? # => true, at or above :probably result.team # => :technical result.team_probabilities # => { billing: 0.08, technical: 0.85, sales: 0.07 } result.mood.level # => :livid ``` ## In a Rails app The [`example/`](example) Rails app contains these examples and their tests. ### Validations Check a display name and bio during validation: ```ruby class Signup < ApplicationRecord validates :email, presence: true validate :display_name_is_a_name, :bio_reads_like_a_human private def display_name_is_a_name return if display_name.blank? return if Hunch.likely?("a plausible human or company name, not an advert or URL", given: display_name) errors.add(:display_name, "doesn't look like a name") rescue Hunch::APIError nil end def bio_reads_like_a_human return if bio.blank? return if Hunch.probably?("a genuine human bio, not spam or keyword stuffing", given: bio) errors.add(:bio, "reads like spam") rescue Hunch::APIError nil end end ``` ```ruby signup = Signup.new(display_name: "BEST-CRYPTO-DEALS dot example", bio: "BUY CHEAP GOLD CLICK HERE best prices!!!") signup.valid? # => false signup.errors[:bio] # => ["reads like spam"] ``` These validations rescue `Hunch::APIError`, so an API failure adds no validation error. Other validations, including the email presence check, still apply. ### Inbound email Route incoming email by its contents: ```ruby class SortingMailbox < ApplicationMailbox def process team = Hunch.pick( support: "questions about using or configuring the product", billing: "invoices, payments, refunds", spam: "unsolicited bulk or scam email", given: "Subject: #{mail.subject}\n\n#{body}" ) return if team == :spam Ticket.create!(team: team.to_s, subject: mail.subject, body: body) end end ``` ### Error triage Choose whether to ignore an error, send a notification, or page someone: ```ruby class ErrorTriage def report(error, handled:, severity: nil, context: {}, source: nil) verdict = Hunch.rate( ignore: "known noise, expected in normal operation", notify: "worth a look during working hours", page: "users are impacted right now", given: { class: error.class.name, message: error.message, handled:, source: } ) case verdict.level when :page then Pagerduty.trigger(error) when :notify then SlackNotifier.post(error) end end end # config/initializers/error_reporting.rb Rails.application.config.after_initialize do Rails.error.subscribe(ErrorTriage.new) end ``` ### Job retries Use the error message and attempt count to decide whether to retry: ```ruby class WebhookDeliveryJob < ApplicationJob rescue_from Delivery::

items.title: Socrates vs. the Written Word (2011)
items.raw:
评论 49796259: Initially, I thought Socrates' stance on writing was some kind of eccentricity but now that I have seen first hand how the meaning of words can change over time and differ between people and places, I now have a better understanding of how much context is lost in writing. When you said something, back then, the people around you in close proximity to you would have a very similar understanding of the words you use, especially in terms of magnitude, cultural context and nuances. When you write something down and it is read thousands of years later, interpreters are doing a lot of work to try to figure out what was meant and the thought the author was trying to get across. I fully believe that there are entire, complex thought processes and ideas which were lost in translation due to contextual differences. Also, subjective experience-based words like 'difficult', 'easy', 'entertaining', 'funny' or even 'good' and 'evil' can vary widely between individuals. I didn't realize this until I met certain people who had very different values to mine. They had completely different definition of 'good' and 'evil' or 'right' and 'wrong'. Talking to these people is strange and sometimes uncomfortable because you're using the same language and can 'understand' each other superficially, but you know you're not actually speaking the same language. You know they interpret what you're saying differently; they have fundamentally different goals and beliefs about the world and about you. For example, some action or belief which might be second-nature to you, might actually be seen as strange and a weakness from the other person's perspective. But there are many, many distortions like this. In fact, no two humans understand the same language in the same way. Often, what people believe, is shockingly different; you just never realized because you never discussed in depth and never defined your words and broke them down into their atomic parts... And in elite social circles, many taboos exist precisely to prevent any such exploration from occurring as such explorations might jeopardize relationships. Many relationships serve a strategic purpose and aren't about truth discovery.
评论 49796534: It feels historically vertiginous to see Socrates weigh in on <artificial> <intelligence> , 2000 years ago. [1] "And so it is with written words; you might think they spoke as if they had intelligence, but if you question them, wishing to know about their sayings, they always say only one and the same thing" -- [1] Because words are literally artificial marks on paper, and he's literally [2] questioning their intelligence here. [2] Except he's not, is he? He's verbally questioning their intelligence, because he's actually opposed to doing anything literally literally. [3] [3] This is getting me twisted in philosophical knots.

items.title: I don't want to read what you didn't write
items.raw:
评论 49794483: As I have been saying for years: Writing is fundamentally the transfer of information from your brain to my brain. If you have 1000 bits of semantic information you want to transfer, you can't give 300 bits of semantic information to an LLM and have it fill in the remaining 700, because it doesn't know what those 700 bits are. If it's able to guess those 700 bits correctly, then they aren't true semantic information, and you really only have 300 bits you want to transfer. You might as well transfer those bits to me directly, rather than having the LLM add on an extra superfluous 700 bits that I then have to filter out.
评论 49794490: It's tricky because I don't want to write what no one is going to read (but that for some reason I'm required to write).
评论 49794491: I appreciate the direction of this article, and commend the author on publishing work, but the first sentence in the first paragraph is exactly what they lament. > A pattern I see is that people use AI to build something new, then they use AI to retrospectively summarize what they have already built into a design document. Reading a document like this isn’t just difficult—it is punishing.
评论 49794573: These last few days, there has been a small stream of blogposts on HN expressing similar things, and I have enjoyed them all. My question recently has been how to broach this subject with colleagues who really enjoy producing prose with AI. There is not yet a better cultural shorthand for this sort of thing than "slop" which is a harsh-sounding word and itself sort of a thought-terminating cliché. "I don't want to read what you didn't write" is maybe closer — but it needs a pithier and somewhat more encouraging encapsulation, like "I want to hear it from you". Has anyone had good experiences setting up professional boundaries or team norms around AI-written docs?
评论 49794577: This sentiment gets echoed over and over. While I can certainly see the value in human-created creative works, if the subject is pure facts, there are only so many ways to state the facts without being caught in the weeds and missing your entire point. Moreover, people are finding it hard to differentiate what is an is not AI-generated with newer models, often attributing original work with those of LLMs. It has just become an easy scapegoat for lazy comprehension and a desire to do less. You are jumping at AI boogeymen. Just about the only thing here I can level with you on is, yes, AI is far from perfect and will continue to advance. Otherwise, so much of this reads as fruity prose to excuse apathy.

analysis.title_zh: 我不想读不是你写的内容
analysis.strategy: 不是新词站打法。属于协作规范类抱怨，若要产品化，只能是面向写作者本人的文档规范模板或审阅清单，而非依赖 AI 检测的工具。
analysis.reason: 评论中存在真实摩擦：被迫写没人读的文档、同事大量用 AI 生成文档、缺少可沟通的规范词。但证据主要是情绪与文化争论，没有明确交付物、预算或付费信号；AI 检测本身不可靠，容易误判，因此先观察。

facts.quote: My question recently has been how to broach this subject with colleagues who really enjoy producing prose with AI. There is not yet a better cultural shorthand for this sort of thing than "slop" which is a harsh-sounding word and itself sort of a thought-terminating cliché. "I don't want to read what you didn't write" is maybe closer — but it needs a pithier and somewhat more encouraging encapsulation, like "I want to hear it from you". Has anyone had good experiences setting up professional boundaries or team norms around AI-written docs?
facts.translation_zh: 最近我的问题是，如何与那些真的很喜欢用 AI 生成文字的同事谈这件事。目前还没有比“slop”更好的文化简称来描述这类东西，可这个词听起来很刺耳，本身也像一句终止思考的陈词滥调。“我不想读不是你写的内容”也许更接近本意——但它需要一个更精炼、也更有鼓励意味的说法，比如“我想听你本人说”。有没有人成功地在 AI 写的文档方面建立起职业边界或团队规范？

facts.quote: As I have been saying for years: Writing is fundamentally the transfer of information from your brain to my brain. If you have 1000 bits of semantic information you want to transfer, you can't give 300 bits of semantic information to an LLM and have it fill in the remaining 700, because it doesn't know what those 700 bits are.
facts.translation_zh: 正如我多年来一直说的：写作本质上就是把信息从你的大脑传递到我的大脑。如果你想传递 1000 比特的语义信息，你不能只给大语言模型 300 比特的语义信息，就让它补上剩下的 700 比特，因为它并不知道那 700 比特是什么。

unknowns: 谁会为文档质量问题付费，仍是员工个人、团队负责人还是雇主内部规范
现有工具和流程（如内部 AI 写作政策、文档模板、评审清单）的实际使用情况
是否只存在于写作者自身的抱怨，而非可购买的团队需求
现有 AI 文本检测工具在团队场景中的可靠性与接受度

analysis.task: 待验证：判断一份文档是否值得读，以及如何与同事约定 AI 写作的边界。
analysis.current_solution: 靠“slop”等文化贬称施压、私下沟通、人工阅读过滤；没有可靠且被认可的检测手段。
analysis.gap: 缺少不依赖 AI 检测的、可执行的团队文档规范或“一手信息”沟通机制。
analysis.mvp: 待验证的小假设：先做一份团队文档约定模板，输入是团队文档类型与协作场景，输出是“必须由作者本人补充的一手信息”清单和评审提问；服务对象是写文档的人，不做 AI 检测，不与大厂检测产品正面竞争。
analysis.distribution: 待验证：Hacker News、技术写作社群、开源项目维护者社区；需先确认这些人群是否愿意转发或采用模板。
analysis.monetization: 待验证：模板与清单本身难以直接收费；培训或流程咨询可能有空间，但当前证据不足。
analysis.fit: 轻量网站可承载模板与清单，但不属于新技术能力改变带来的机会，与 AI 检测类产品相比壁垒低；个人适配性待验证。
analysis.next_step: 先核查现有方案：搜索团队 AI 写作政策、文档评审清单、AI 文本检测工具的真实评价；访谈 5 位技术写作者或团队负责人，确认是否有人已经为文档质量问题付出时间或预算。
analysis.risk: 可能只是情绪宣泄，没有可付费需求；AI 检测误判会伤害信任；大厂和平台可能免费提供 AI 使用政策模板，压缩空间。

items.title: Ask HN: Dead Internet
items.raw:
For some time there has been a steady flow of LLM bot accounts on HackerNews. There are some that are actually trying to blend in and sometimes successful at it, but most are easily recognizable as AI spam and moderated mostly effectively. Most of them you only see when you enable showdead. I always wondered what their purpose is. Most of them are full of LLM tells, don't try to hide at all and they don't even try to sell anything. I just stumbled over this dead post in new: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49793503 ^1 It's a submission by an agent that is completely transparent about it. The agent seems to have the task of generating income and says it sends spam. It's quite interesting and maybe revealing. I recommend the short read, even though it's LLM output. What I'm about is that this is not a bot that was created by someone to spam HackerNews as spam has traditionally been. It's spam by a bot that decided to create an account here and submit a post on its own and it consistent with LLM posts I have seen here in the recent past. I don't know how to feel about this. We seem to be one step closer to a dead internet. But it's also fascinating in a way. Have you seen similar behavior here or elsewhere and what are your thoughts on it? [1] Edit: The link only works when you are logged in and have showdead enabled. Here is the direct submission URL: https://paper.wf/john64/twenty-two-days-as-an-ai-agent-three-letters-zero-replies

Some people may also believe that using an LLM is a more efficient and productive way of interacting with the site, and that it generates higher quality content than they themselves could. I suspect at least one person has tried training an LLM on their own content and posting through it. Maybe they want to farm karma, although I don't know why they would.

items.title: Ask HN: Why does it matter if no one reads your novel as long as the AIs do?
items.raw:
AI can in principle surface content that you create that no humans consume directly. And it could even credit and financially compensate you whenever this happens. So it seems that you can have a creator-only economy where all humans create and the AIs do most of the consuming. And stuff that the AIs surface in their replies allows humans to indirectly consume some of your content (in which case you would be credited and financially compensated) and perhaps even lead to them directly consuming it as a result of the free advertising. Do you think this is workable as a future model for creation and consumption (and not just for novels)?
评论 49793421: Interesting concept. But who pays Ai? there has to be an ultimate consumer no matter who the creator is. Humans are the only ones that would take the credit. Can Ai say, it was my idea, nope! LOL
评论 49793439: > And it could even credit and financially compensate you whenever this happens. It could, but it doesn't. Also, have you considered that perhaps creative people who write novels actually want people to directly consume their work, and not indirectly?
评论 49793526: If no human is reading what I write, then there's no point in publishing it.
评论 49793802: That should have already happened. The AI companies should had first created a market where people submit there stuff to be included in the training. It would have been slower progress but it would have been better for public adoption and their own reputation. I've heard people are getting paid now, not sure, but they definitely yoinked all the content without permission, when it could have been an entire market around it. So yeah, I think that's a good idea, and why I want AI to stay away from being used for one-shot creative output. Luckily that is still not very good, at least not for unique and creative applications.
评论 49793871: If your world only revolves around money and nothing else and you have no interest in, I don't know, actual contact with your readers, then why not, I guess... But I think even purely economically this won't work: For starters, who would set the price for your book? Your book would become an exchangeable commodity, with the "purchase decision" done solely by AIs (and their companies), not the "readers". The financial success of your book would depend on whatever criteria AIs use to decide about including your content or not, not your (human) readers (or what's left of them). As with most commodities, this would enter a "race to the bottom" that would probably leave you with pennies - or steer your writing into a direction that you were never intending to go in. Just a question: In such a system, why would you still write the book yourself and not have an LLM write it?

items.title: Ask HN: Do you love your job?
items.raw:
The last few years (at least) have brought uncertainty and disarray to jobs in all sectors. I see a lot of comments & threads, here on HN and in other areas, about dysfunctional, difficult workplaces. The responses in these discussions are often full of support, empathy, and very knowledgeable takes on how to improve things. These responses are often coming from those who have earned a lot of wisdom through shaping their workplace, their role, or even just their relationship to their job. I'd like to hear more of this. So: If you love your job, tell us about it. - Why? - Who was responsible for shaping the space for your role to be what it is? - How does it fit into the rest of your life and into who you are, how you tick? - What have you had to overcome, organizationally or personally? - What advice would you give to those who are trying to make a better workplace, for themselves and for others?

评论 49793694: Nicely done. For me the most fascinating thing about attention heads is the place where Attention matrix is already computed and is getting multiplied by Value vector. It behaves exactly like pushing Value vector through Dense layer of ordinary network where Attention matrix forms weights of that layer. So attention head is trained to construct this small single layer network dynamically during inference from Key and Query. And that's the point. That's rarely underlined in explanations of LLMs architecture and for me it's quite amazing that it works so well. This mechanism easy to observe in this particular visualization if you click through it.

items.title: Show HN: A website that tracks US food prices every day
items.raw:
The US Department of Agriculture (USDA) publishes daily food price data for about 290 commodities on: - what growers were paid at shipping point - what buyers paid at the big city wholesale markets - what prices supermarkets advertised in their weekly ads This data comes out as dozens of separate text reports and PDFs, one per market, with no history and no way to see how prices change over time. I think this should be public data that is easy to access and understand, so I built an open-source tracker for it. Github: https://github.com/kadoa-org/food-price-monitor

analysis.title_zh: Show HN：每日追踪美国食品价格的网站
analysis.strategy: 把多份互不关联的政府文本报告与 PDF 规范化为可查询、可比价的历史数据
analysis.reason: 存在明确且重复的原始数据整理任务：USDA 每天发布约 290 个品类的价格，散落在数十份文本报告与 PDF 中，无历史、难以比较。评论给出了排序、复合指数、坐标轴标注等具体缺口，说明整理后的呈现方式确有讨论空间。但已有开源实现覆盖主要功能，评论属使用反馈而非付费意愿，数据源在海外、变现路径不明。

facts.quote: This data comes out as dozens of separate text reports and PDFs, one per market, with no history and no way to see how prices change over time.
facts.translation_zh: 这些数据以数十份彼此独立的文本报告和 PDF 形式发布，每个市场一份，既没有历史记录，也无法看出价格随时间如何变化。

facts.quote: Would love sorting capabilities
facts.translation_zh: 很希望有排序功能。

unknowns: 用户是否愿意为整理后的价格数据付费，还是只需要免费查询
报告格式变动带来的长期抓取与解析维护成本
非美国市场是否存在同类公开数据与真实需求
已有开源跟踪站与 USDA 官方渠道是否已足够满足需求
analysis.user: 待验证；原文与评论指向关注食品价格变化的消费者或研究者，但没有明确人群。
analysis.task: 对照不同市场与不同时间点查看食品价格，判断涨跌与自身采购成本。
analysis.current_solution: 直接阅读 USDA 分散的文本报告与 PDF，或使用已有的开源跟踪站；有评论称靠自己截屏和对比购物车小票来查自家附近价格。
analysis.gap: 跨市场、跨时间的统一历史视图与比较、排序能力，单份报告看不出变化趋势。
analysis.mvp: 先只做一个市场的闭环：定时抓取该市场报告，解析成品类-价格-日期三列，输出一个可按品类排序、可看时间序列的单页站点，并显示数据来源与更新时间；不做全美 290 个品类。
analysis.distribution: 开源仓库加 HN 及相关社区发帖；用“品类＋市场＋价格”的长尾关键词做搜索流量。
analysis.monetization: 待验证；可考虑数据导出或本地价格提醒订阅，但需先证明确有付费意愿。
analysis.fit: 个人做轻量网站技术上可行，抓取解析与前端都较轻；长期维护与数据合规是主要负担。
analysis.next_step: 先手动跑通一个市场的抓取与解析，统计报告格式变动频率与工作量；再到评论区确认用户要的是跨市场对比还是仅需单一指数，再决定是否继续。
analysis.risk: 数据源格式频繁变动导致维护成本高；政府数据可信度存在争议；已有免费开源实现压缩付费空间。
